vignette: Arjun was thirty-two when the mugging occurred. He was leaving the parish hall after conducting a late-night pastoral visit when a man stepped from the brick alley behind the building. The attacker swung without warning, his knuckles scraping against Arjun’s shoulder as a baton cracked against his temple. What remained were not coherent narratives, but sudden, high-definition snapshots: the glint of a silver ring, the damp, sour smell of tobacco and wet asphalt, the relentless, heavy breathing of the assailant echoing long after the footsteps had faded. In the weeks that followed, the sensory fragments refused to stay buried. The moment Arjun encountered a crowded street or overheard a stranger’s labored breath, his mind would instantly replay the attacker’s coat, and with it came a suffocating wave of rage that tightened his chest until he could barely breathe. Because he felt fundamentally helpless against life’s cruelty, he began to cancel his pastoral visits and stopped leading the evening vigils. He found himself watching the exits of coffee shops, his eyes darting to every man who approached too quickly, the heavy breath of a jogger past his office window sending his pulse racing to his throat. The self-blame tightened his avoidance, pushing him further into isolation. Yet every time he shut his eyes to rest, the unbidden images would surface, sharp and relentless. His belief that he was inherently flawed did not remain abstract; it fed directly into the intrusions, causing his mind to reconstruct the assault with relentless, punitive clarity. The rage that followed these memories felt like undeniable proof that he was uniquely destined to attract danger, deepening his certainty that he could never stop bad things from happening to him. The closer a crowd grew, the more the phantom pressure of the attacker’s grip returned, and the more convinced he became that his own inadequacy had made him a target. The parishioners noticed his sudden withdrawal, whispering about his absence, but Arjun could only focus on the next doorway, the next heavy exhale, the next shadow. Now, at thirty-four, Arjun sits in a quiet clinic waiting room, his hands folded tightly in his lap. The weight of his widowed status has compounded his exhaustion; his wife, Priya, had held him together through the early months, but his constant tension and sudden eruptions of anger had pushed her to her limits before her own illness took her. He is terrified that if he opens the door to therapy, he will be forced to face the full weight of his guilt, that he will lose the fragile control he has built around his avoidance. He wants to return to the pulpit, to sit among his parishioners without scanning for threats, but he fears that without intervention, he will remain trapped in a cycle of his own making, forever waiting for the next attack to begin.
